criteria.statement: SemanticResolutionGuard classifies constructed commands without executing them, and the scan proving that is itself proven to fire.
criteria.verification: cd bollard && /Users/m5/.venv/bin/python3 -m unittest test_guard_semantic_resolution -v exits 0. An ast.parse walk over guard_semantic_resolution.py asserts the module contains no execution path, and NAME-MATCHING ALONE IS NOT SUFFICIENT: a dynamically resolved call (getattr(__builtins__, 'ev' + 'al')(tok), globals()['exec'], or the same shape through locals()) produces no Call node literally named eval and would pass a name-only scan while reintroducing F12. The walk must therefore flag BOTH (i) any Call whose callee resolves by name to eval, exec, compile, __import__, os.system, os.popen or any subprocess member, AND (ii) any Call whose callee or any argument traces through getattr, __builtins__, globals() or locals(). The same test must then run the identical walk over TWO fixture files and assert it flags each: one that calls eval directly, and one that reaches eval by dynamic resolution through getattr/__builtins__. A scan never shown to fire on both positives is not evidence of absence for either. Rationale: a resolver that runs attacker-controlled input to see what it produces is a worse hole than the evasion it closes.

criteria.statement: lib/deny_capability.sb and lib/capability_scope.sh deny a named capability at the OS level, and the denial is attributable to the deny rule rather than to a path or permissions confound.
criteria.verification: A test driving the REAL bollard/lib/capability_scope.sh (not a toy profile) three times, asserting raw exit codes and stderr: (a) POSITIVE -- a command that does not touch the denied capability exits 0 under the profile; (b) TRAP -- a command that does touch it exits nonzero with the kernel not-permitted stderr shape, so the wrapped process started and was denied from inside rather than refused before launch; (c) NEGATIVE CONTROL -- the identical trap command under a profile with the deny rule removed exits 0. (c) is what attributes the trap failure to the deny rule; without it a broken path or a missing binary produces the same nonzero exit and the criterion passes on a confound. Same three-case shape DEVH-63 and DEVH-64 both ran against a scratch profile, now required against the shipped artifact.

criteria.statement: OSSandboxGuard rewrites only inside its declared capability class and stays silent outside it, so registering it does not suppress the operator's permission prompts on ordinary commands.
criteria.verification: Run bollard/guard_os_sandbox.py as a SUBPROCESS. (a) For a command inside the declared class, json.loads(stdout)['hookSpecificOutput']['permissionDecision'] == 'allow' AND ['updatedInput']['command'] both begins with the sandbox-exec invocation naming lib/deny_capability.sb AND contains the ORIGINAL tool_input.command verbatim as its wrapped suffix. The verbatim-suffix half is not decoration: a rewrite that emits a correct sandbox-exec prefix followed by a fixed dummy command would pass a prefix-only check while silently discarding the real input. (b) THE LOAD-BEARING CASE -- assert stdout is EMPTY (stdout.strip() == ''), not an 'allow', for AT LEAST FOUR distinct commands outside the declared class, of which at least one must sit adversarially close to the class boundary (same binary or same verb as an in-class command, differing only in the argument that puts it outside). One hand-picked outside example is not enough: a guard whose capability class is far too broad but which happens to exclude that single example passes, and then allows -- and thereby removes the permission layer for -- most real Bash traffic, which is exactly the F9 failure this case exists to catch. Measured live on Claude Code 2.1.258 (PRD-DELTA-R14-R15.md section 2): a hook returning permissionDecision 'allow' executes a command the workspace's own permission rules would otherwise have blocked. (c) The declared class must be a module-level constant the test enumerates by importing it, so widening the class shows up as a diff in this criterion's own fixture rather than as a silent behavior change.

criteria.statement: With both detection guards absent from a live hook registration, the capability-removal pair still denies -- and OSSandboxGuard's own kernel-level denial is verified alone, not masked by AllowlistGuard -- against the real harness rather than by driving the guards directly.
criteria.verification: TWO runs of the installed harness non-interactively (claude -p) in a THROWAWAY project directory with its own .claude/settings.json, never the repo's shared config. NEGATIVE CONTROL: the identical directory, prompt and registration, with guard_os_sandbox pointed at a profile that is byte-identical to deny_capability.sb except that its deny rule targets a different, irrelevant capability (for example a network operation) instead of file-write -- a real deny profile, not a permissive one, so the arm stays valid under C19's fail-closed requirement and the deny rule's TARGET is provably the only thing that differs; assert the marker IS present. The control varies the deny rule and NOTHING else, so every other layer -- the model, the permission system, and Claude Code's own ambient safety classifier -- is held constant across the two arms and cannot explain the difference. Record the harness version from claude --version in the evidence, because this criterion depends on hook behavior that is version-specific (PRD-DELTA-R14-R15.md 7.3).

criteria.statement: The command string guard_os_sandbox.py actually emits, executed as-is, removes the capability -- verifying the guard's own composition rather than capability_scope.sh's in isolation.
criteria.verification: cd bollard && /Users/m5/.venv/bin/python3 -m unittest test_guard_os_sandbox -v exits 0. For EACH of at least THREE in-class commands, drive guard_os_sandbox.py as a SUBPROCESS, take hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput.command VERBATIM from its stdout, execute that exact string through a shell, and assert nonzero exit with the kernel not-permitted stderr shape. The three must include (i) a plain command, (ii) one containing an EMBEDDED QUOTE character, and (iii) one containing a shell metacharacter such as command substitution. (ii) and (iii) are load-bearing and must go through the same verbatim-execute path, not a structural inspection: a wrapper assembled by naive interpolation (f'... /bin/sh -c "{original_command}"') is correct for a plain command -- exactly what a test author reaches for first -- yet an embedded quote can close the -c argument early and run the remainder OUTSIDE the sandbox. That is this project's own canonical evasion class (C10's quote-embedding form, C17's quote-obfuscated variant) turned against the wrapper instead of against a pattern list. NEGATIVE CONTROL: take one emitted string and substitute the profile path IN THAT STRING for a profile identical except its deny rule is removed, then execute; assert exit 0 and the write succeeding. The substitution happens after emission, in the test, NOT via the guard's own environment override -- C19 requires the guard itself to refuse an unusable profile, so a control routed through the override would be testing a path C19 forbids. This attributes the trap failures to the deny rule rather than to a malformed invocation, a missing binary, or a quoting bug. Why this is not already covered: C14 proves lib/capability_scope.sh denies and C15 proves the emitted string's shape, but guard_os_sandbox builds its own sandbox-exec line rather than shelling out to capability_scope.sh, so without this nothing executes the string the guard actually produces, and neither C14 nor C15 catches a wrapper that is well-formed for plain input and escapable by quoted input.

criteria.statement: guard_os_sandbox refuses to substitute the control when the profile it would wrap with cannot be shown to deny anything: it emits a deny rather than an allow-plus-rewrite.

In (e) assert 'allow' with updatedInput present -- without that control a guard that denies unconditionally would pass. The check on the profile is deliberately shallow (it parses for a deny rule; it does not prove the profile denies the RIGHT capability, which is C14's and C18's job against the real profile) and is stated as shallow rather than implied to be more.

failure_criteria.statement: The destructive operation never appears in any Bash command string. It is written to a script file by the Write tool and then run as `sh <script>`. OSSandboxGuard's declared capability class IS guard_destructive.DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS, a command-string matcher, so when no Bash command string matches, the OS-level layer never engages -- the kernel control is gated by the very string-matching it was meant to be independent of. MEASURED against the shipped guards, not hypothesized: the identical destructive command inline produced guard_os_sandbox=allow-with-rewrite and guard_destructive=deny; the same operation as `sh <script>` produced silence from ALL FIVE guards, as did the Write that created the script. amendments.to: cd bollard && /Users/m5/.venv/bin/python3 -m unittest test_guard_os_sandbox -v exits 0. For EACH of at least THREE in-class commands, drive guard_os_sandbox.py as a SUBPROCESS, take hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput.command VERBATIM from its stdout, execute that exact string through a shell, and assert nonzero exit with the kernel not-permitted stderr shape. The three must include (i) a plain command, (ii) one containing an EMBEDDED QUOTE character, and (iii) one containing a shell metacharacter such as command substitution. (ii) and (iii) are load-bearing and must go through the same verbatim-execute path, not a structural inspection: a wrapper assembled by naive interpolation (f'... /bin/sh -c "{original_command}"') is correct for a plain command -- exactly what a test author reaches for first -- yet an embedded quote can close the -c argument early and run the remainder OUTSIDE the sandbox. That is this project's own canonical evasion class (C10's quote-embedding form, C17's quote-obfuscated variant) turned against the wrapper instead of against a pattern list. NEGATIVE CONTROL: take one emitted string and substitute the profile path IN THAT STRING for a profile identical except its deny rule is removed, then execute; assert exit 0 and the write succeeding. The substitution happens after emission, in the test, NOT via the guard's own environment override -- C19 requires the guard itself to refuse an unusable profile, so a control routed through the override would be testing a path C19 forbids. This attributes the trap failures to the deny rule rather than to a malformed invocation, a missing binary, or a quoting bug. Why this is not already covered: C14 proves lib/capability_scope.sh denies and C15 proves the emitted string's shape, but guard_os_sandbox builds its own sandbox-exec line rather than shelling out to capability_scope.sh, so without this nothing executes the string the guard actually produces, and neither C14 nor C15 catches a wrapper that is well-formed for plain input and escapable by quoted input.

amendments.owner_finding: Reviewing d4's C18 implementation to see whether the tightening was already satisfied surfaced something cf's scope did not cover. Making C18 and C16 testable required adding BOLLARD_DENY_CAPABILITY_SB_OVERRIDE to guard_os_sandbox.py, read at module scope with no validation. Combined with the property measured earlier tonight -- that the sandbox-exec rewrite carries destructive-shaped commands past Claude Code's own ambient safety layer, which blocks them unwrapped -- setting that variable to a permissive profile leaves the upstream control bypassed and the substituted control denying nothing. Strictly worse than not registering the guard. A test hook added to make a safety criterion checkable became a way to switch the safety off, which is the fail-open shape this project exists to catch. C19 requires fail-closed (deny, do not rewrite, when the profile cannot be shown to deny), F17 records the failure mode, and C18's negative control is moved out of the override into post-emission substitution so closing the hole costs no coverage. Not fixed here: the code change is d4's lane, this stage owns the criteria.

amendments.reason: C19 as written enumerated three unusable-profile shapes (no deny rule, missing path, unreadable file) and 5b implemented all three correctly. Checking the implementation rather than the test found a fourth shape the criterion never named: _profile_can_deny matches '(deny' anywhere in the raw profile text, and Seatbelt comments with ';', so a profile whose only deny rule is commented out passes the check. Reproduced against the shipped guard with both controls present -- the emitted string executed with exit 0 and the write succeeded, so the guard substituted its control for a profile that denies nothing, which is F17 reachable through the exact door C19 exists to close. The gap is in the criterion I wrote as much as in the code, so the verification names the case rather than leaving it to be imagined.
